title: CML vs Leukemoid Reaction: Lazy Clone, Angry Reaction
summary: Separate chronic myeloid leukaemia from a leukemoid reaction using the smear pattern (myelocyte peak and basophilia vs late forms and toxic changes), the historical LAP/NAP score, and the deciding BCR::ABL1 test.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 34 Hit 1 (core: CML = t(9;22) BCR::ABL1, TKI therapy, basophilia, low NAP), Trap 1 (leukemoid reaction vs CML) and the Figure 34 anchor. Checked against Abukhiran 2020 and Tungjitviboonkun 2026. Added context: the LAP/NAP score is rarely used now that BCR::ABL1 testing is available. Pending: “leukocyte count often > 30 × 10⁹/L”.

objectives: Describe granulocyte maturation and what a left shift and a leukemoid reaction are.
Contrast the smear features of CML and a leukemoid reaction.
Explain the roles of BCR::ABL1 testing and the LAP/NAP score, and link BCR::ABL1 to TKI therapy.

scenes.title: Two patients, one smear pattern
scenes.altText: Two patient cards, both with WBC 80 × 10⁹/L and a left shift (immature granulocytes in the blood). Patient A has severe pneumonia; patient B feels tired and has an enlarged spleen. Both smears look busy with immature cells. A question: same disease?

cues.text: Two patients both have a white cell count of 80 billion per litre, with immature granulocytes in the blood — a left shift.
One has severe pneumonia. The other is tired, with an enlarged spleen.
Is one a leukaemia and the other a reaction? The smear alone can fool you.

scenes.title: Normal: the neutrophil ladder and a left shift
scenes.altText: A maturation ladder: myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → segmented neutrophil. Normally only bands and segs leave the marrow. During infection or other stress, signals such as G-CSF push the marrow to release earlier forms: a left shift, usually of late precursors (bands, metamyelocytes, some myelocytes). A leukemoid reaction is a marked reactive leukocytosis (one definition: > 40 × 10⁹/L) without a blood cancer.

cues.text: Neutrophils mature in steps in the marrow: blast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and finally the segmented neutrophil.
Normally, only bands and segmented neutrophils are released into the blood.
Under stress — infection, inflammation, some tumours — signals such as G-C-S-F push the marrow to release earlier forms too. That’s a left shift.
When the reaction is extreme — one definition is above 40 billion per litre — and there’s no blood cancer, it’s called a leukemoid reaction.

props.label: Stress signals (e.g. G-CSF) → release earlier forms

scenes.title: What changes: a clone vs a reaction
scenes.altText: Left, CML: a stem-cell clone with the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation — the Philadelphia chromosome — fuses BCR and ABL1 into a constantly active tyrosine kinase. Its blood shows the whole ladder with a myelocyte peak and basophilia (illustrative bar chart). Right, leukemoid reaction: late forms dominate (bands, segs), with few early precursors and no basophilia; neutrophils show toxic granulation, Döhle bodies and vacuoles.

cues.text: Chronic myeloid leukaemia starts with one stem cell. Chromosomes 9 and 22 swap pieces — the Philadelphia chromosome — fusing BCR to ABL1. The fusion protein is a tyrosine kinase that’s always switched on.
The clone fills the blood with every stage of the ladder. Typically there’s a myelocyte peak — and basophils are increased.
In a leukemoid reaction, late forms dominate: bands and segmented neutrophils, with few early precursors and no basophilia.
And the reactive neutrophils look stressed: toxic granulation, Döhle bodies and vacuoles.

scenes.title: In the lab: BCR::ABL1 settles it
scenes.altText: Test cards. BCR::ABL1 by PCR or FISH, done on peripheral blood, confirms CML. The older leukocyte (neutrophil) alkaline phosphatase score is low in CML and high in reactive neutrophilia, but it lacks specificity and is rarely used now that BCR::ABL1 testing is widely available. Treatment card: tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib target the BCR::ABL1 kinase.

cues.text: Today, the deciding test is molecular. PCR or FISH for BCR::ABL1 — which can be done on peripheral blood — confirms chronic myeloid leukaemia.
The older test was the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score, also called NAP or LAP. It’s low in CML and high in reactive neutrophilia, like infection.
But many things affect it and it isn’t specific, so it’s rarely used now that BCR::ABL1 testing is available.
Finding BCR::ABL1 also points to treatment: tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib block the fusion kinase.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “WBC 80 with left shift = CML” is crossed out → “Check basophils, myelocyte peak and toxic changes; confirm with BCR::ABL1.” Trap card: “High LAP/NAP = CML” is crossed out → “LAP/NAP is LOW in CML, high in reactions.” Trap card: “LAP/NAP is the definitive test” is crossed out → “BCR::ABL1 is.”

cues.text: Trap one: a very high count with a left shift is not automatically CML. Look for basophilia and a myelocyte peak versus toxic changes — and confirm with BCR::ABL1.
Trap two: in CML the LAP or NAP score is low. A high score fits a reaction.
Trap three: the LAP score isn’t definitive. BCR::ABL1 testing is.

scenes.title: Lazy clone, angry reaction
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “CML neutrophils are lazy (low NAP) and bring basophil friends; reactive neutrophils are angry (toxic granules, high NAP) and come alone.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: CML neutrophils are lazy — low NAP — and bring basophil friends. Reactive neutrophils are angry — toxic granules, high NAP — and come alone.

Where it breaks: reactions can occasionally show basophilia, anaemia or low platelets; the NAP score is affected by many factors; some CML presentations are atypical; and the Philadelphia chromosome also occurs in some acute leukaemias.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “CML = t(9;22) BCR::ABL1 clone: myelocyte peak, basophilia, low NAP, TKI therapy”, “Leukemoid reaction = reactive: late forms, toxic changes, high NAP — BCR::ABL1 negative”.

cues.text: CML is a BCR::ABL1 clone with a myelocyte peak, basophilia and low NAP, treated with kinase inhibitors; a leukemoid reaction is reactive, with late forms and toxic changes — BCR::ABL1 testing decides.

props.label: CML: BCR::ABL1 clone · myelocyte peak · basophils · low NAP
Leukemoid: late forms · toxic changes · high NAP · BCR::ABL1 neg.

explanation.what: Plain language: CML is a blood cancer from one faulty stem cell; a leukemoid reaction is the marrow’s extreme but normal response to stress. Scientific terms: CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by t(9;22)(q34;q11) producing the BCR::ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase; a leukemoid reaction is a reactive leukocytosis (one definition > 40 × 10⁹/L) without haematologic malignancy, often cytokine-driven (e.g. G-CSF).
explanation.why: A constitutively active kinase drives clonal expansion of all granulocytic stages (myelocyte peak, basophilia); cytokine-driven reactions release mainly late precursors from a normal marrow, with toxic changes in activated neutrophils.
explanation.measure: BCR::ABL1 by PCR or FISH (peripheral blood suffices) confirms CML. LAP/NAP score is low in CML and high in reactive neutrophilia, but is non-specific and rarely used now. Smear: CML — full spectrum, myelocyte peak, basophilia; reaction — bands/segs predominate, few early precursors, no basophilia, toxic granulation, Döhle bodies, vacuoles.
explanation.differs: Clonal (BCR::ABL1-positive, low NAP, basophilia) vs reactive (BCR::ABL1-negative, high NAP, toxic changes); historical NAP score vs modern molecular testing.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the classic “high WBC, left shift — CML or leukemoid?” question with NAP and basophils as clues, t(9;22) BCR::ABL1, and imatinib.

right.label: Leukemoid reaction
points: Late forms, toxic changes, high NAP

questions.stem: A patient with severe infection has WBC 80 × 10⁹/L with a left shift, toxic granulation, Döhle bodies, no basophilia and a high NAP score. What is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Toxic changes, absent basophilia and a high NAP fit a reactive leukocytosis.
Incorrect. CML typically shows basophilia, a myelocyte peak and a low NAP.
Incorrect. Nothing suggests a blast-predominant process.
Incorrect. PV is defined by raised red cell mass, not a reactive left shift.

questions.stem: Which test best confirms chronic myeloid leukaemia?

options.rationale: Correct. The BCR::ABL1 fusion defines CML and can be detected in peripheral blood.
Incorrect. It is low in CML but non-specific and rarely used now.
Incorrect. B12 may rise in myeloproliferative disease but does not confirm CML.
Incorrect. A high count is not specific.

questions.stem: Why is imatinib effective in chronic myeloid leukaemia?

options.text: It inhibits the constitutively active BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase
options.rationale: Correct. Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting the fusion protein.
Incorrect. That describes ATRA in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
Incorrect. Treatment is not aimed at the NAP score.
Incorrect. Purine analogues are used in other diseases, such as hairy cell leukaemia.

claims.text: CML: t(9;22)(q34;q11) BCR::ABL1 constitutive tyrosine kinase; full granulocytic spectrum with myelocyte peak and basophilia; TKIs (imatinib).
Leukemoid reaction: reactive leukocytosis (e.g. > 40 × 10⁹/L) without malignancy; late precursors; toxic granulation, Döhle bodies, vacuoles; no basophilia.
LAP/NAP low in CML, high in reactions; non-specific and rarely used now; BCR::ABL1 on peripheral blood confirms.
